rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figs 4-7; the authors set up a sensor-based (TDT, piezometer, datalogger) automated sprinkler control system in the Padova Botanical Garden and report its first-year (2000) operation, soil moisture and matric potential data.
rows.notes: The study reports the technical/operational performance of a soil-moisture-sensor automated irrigation controller: it terminated irrigation when rainfall raised moisture above the full point, sensors responded within 2 min, average water status was favourable, and the 'average' criterion penalised plants with higher needs. It does not measure or compare water use against a non-automated baseline, so it gives no result of its own on water conservation; irrigation volumes (200-250 mm; >450 mm) are reported without any saving estimate. Functioning automation is only a precondition of the claimed conservation effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figs 4-7; own set-up and first-year monitoring of an automated irrigation system in the Padova Botanical Garden.
rows.notes: The irrigation network consists of about 550 sprinklers controlled by 27 solenoid valves (Section 2.2); no drip irrigation is involved, and no water-saving result is reported in any case. The study is about sensor-based automation of sprinkler irrigation in a heterogeneous garden.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a single-site case study (one 2 ha garden, one season) describing system design and first-year operational performance; it contains no water-use comparison or savings quantification.
